messages.subject: Combining multilevel and item-response models
parts:
Hi all,

I am building a model that combines a IRT model - to measure the latent trait outcome variable - and a set of varying intercept predictors (much like the election88 example). The idea is for something like a structural equation model. 

I began by building and testing each model separately (using an additive scale as the outcome variable for the multilevel model). So far so good. However, I am stumped as to how to combine the two. Specifically, I gather from reading some exchanges on this list that the ability parameter of the IRT model - which I call theta - requires a normal(0, 1) prior to resolve the additive offset identification problem. But theta is is also my outcome variable, so I also want theta to be sampled from a normal(theta_hat, sigma_theta) distribution, where theta_hat is the vector of fitted values from the MLM.

Any suggestions?

> reading some exchanges on this list that the ability parameter of the IRT model - which I call theta - requires a
> normal(0, 1) prior to resolve the additive offset identification problem. But theta is is also my outcome variable, so I
> also want theta to be sampled from a normal(theta_hat, sigma_theta) distribution, where theta_hat is the vector of

>

Funny -- Andrew and I were just discussing this today, so maybe he'll
weigh in if I mess up my recollection of what we discussed. The main
issue that came up is that normal(0,1) prior is a hack in that it
centers the abilities, but they're not still not identified in the population.
That is, if you add or subtract students, the values will change (though not
in expecation).

The second thing that came up is that by fixing one
of the abilities to 0, you do identify the population in that everyone's
ability is scaled to the student with the ability pinned to 0. Still not
very nice if you want a more "natural" interpretation of the parameters. But
the simple fact is that the model's not identified by just

discrimination[j] * (ability[i] - difficulty[j])

Fixing the prior of ability to normal(0,1) deals with both the
multiplicative and additive non-identifiability. The choice of 0
and 1 are arbitrary here, but you might as well use those because
they're standard and it works well for Stan's sampling scale and default
inits.

For the additive non-identifiability, you can either pin down
the location of the ability OR the difficulty parameters. For the
multiplicative identifiability, you need to pin down the scale of
one or the other.

You can also set one of the abilities to 0 or one of the difficulties
to 0, but that's clunky to code.

If you're using a predictor theta_hat, you can avoid using an intercept
term in theta_hat --- if you add an intecept there, it's just another
additive term that's not identified. It then pushes the problem of
scale identifiability up to the prior on the slopes.

You could also set sigma_theta = 1 to deal with the scale issue, though I've
often found in a hierarchical model having a reasonable prior on sigma_theta
will do exactly the same thing.

- Bob

Thanks for the very thorough and helpful reply Bob. 

Setting the scale of the ability prior to 1 is one of those obvious things that just didn't occur to me. So that provides the scale and a prior on the difficulty parameters provides the location, with the expectation of the ability prior being the fitted values from the MLM, which then joins the two models together.
